title: Chapter 2 Mastery Quiz: Ethics & Human Participant Protections
description: Demonstrate comprehensive mastery of the Belmont Report, IRBs, informed consent, deception rules, and research integrity.

questions.question: Which historical event directly led to the establishment of the Nuremberg Code of 1947?

options.text: The Stanford Prison Experiment
Atrocities committed in medical experiments on prisoners in Nazi concentration camps
The discovery of penicillin
Milgram's obedience experiments

questions.explanation: The Nuremberg Code was drafted after the Doctors' Trial in Nuremberg to hold Nazi medical experimenters accountable and protect human subjects.

questions.question: What was the central ethical violation in the Tuskegee Syphilis Study?

options.text: Participants were given an experimental vaccine without FDA clearance
Effective penicillin antibiotic treatment was deliberately withheld from infected men for decades
Researchers published participant names in local newspapers
Participants were forced to run marathons while sick

questions.explanation: Researchers tracked the natural progression of syphilis by deliberately withholding known, effective penicillin treatment from poor African American men.

questions.question: Which core principle of the Belmont Report requires treating individuals as autonomous agents capable of making their own decisions?

options.text: Beneficence
Respect for Persons
Justice
Operationalism

questions.explanation: Respect for Persons demands that individuals be treated as autonomous beings who can choose whether or not to participate in research.

questions.question: The Belmont principle of Beneficence obligates psychological researchers to:

options.text: Ensure that the benefits of research exceed risks and that participants are protected from harm
Distribute research findings exclusively to paying subscribers
Pay every participant at least $100 per hour
Never use statistical significance testing

questions.explanation: Beneficence encompasses the duty to 'do no harm' and maximize potential benefits while minimizing potential risks.

questions.question: Which Belmont principle was severely violated in the Tuskegee Study by selecting only vulnerable, impoverished African American men to bear the health burdens of research?

options.text: Justice
Parsimony
Falsifiability
Empiricism

questions.explanation: The principle of Justice requires fair distribution of research burdens and benefits; exploiting a vulnerable subpopulation violates Justice.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

options.text: To decide which research will be awarded Nobel prizes
To review research proposals involving human participants and protect their rights and welfare
To review the grammar and stylistic formatting of journal manuscripts
To manage university tuition billing

questions.explanation: IRBs are federally mandated committees tasked with reviewing research protocols to safeguard human subjects' welfare and rights.

questions.question: Research involving completely anonymous surveys on benign topics with healthy adults typically receives which category of IRB review?

options.text: Exempt Review
Full Board Review
IACUC Veterinary Review
Subpoena Review

questions.explanation: Anonymous surveys involving negligible risk to healthy adults are classified as Exempt from full board oversight.

questions.question: Which of the following studies would strictly require a Full Board IRB review?

options.text: An anonymous web poll about favorite colors
An experimental trial testing trauma recall using high-stress induction in prison inmates
A teacher evaluating standard math curriculum test scores in an existing classroom
A consumer satisfaction survey for a grocery store

questions.explanation: Involving high-risk stress induction and a vulnerable population (prisoners) mandates a rigorous Full Board IRB review.

questions.question: What constitutes 'coercion' in the context of informed consent?

options.text: Providing clear written explanations of study procedures
Exerting undue influence or pressure such that an individual feels unable to freely decline participation
Requiring participants to sign their legal names
Offering free parking validation at the university clinic

questions.explanation: Coercion involves implicit or explicit threats of penalty or excessively irresistible rewards that compromise autonomous choice.

questions.question: Under APA guidelines, when is deception in research ethically permissible?

options.text: Whenever it makes an experiment more entertaining for the researcher
Only when justified by significant scientific value, no effective alternative exists, and it does not involve severe pain or trauma
Whenever the participants are college students
Deception is strictly prohibited under every circumstance with zero exceptions

questions.explanation: APA ethics permit deception only when scientifically justified, non-deceptive methods cannot work, and participants are debriefed afterward.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the debriefing process in psychological studies?

options.text: To convince participants to recruit their friends for the study
To explain the true purpose of the research, disclose any deception, and restore psychological equilibrium
To grade participants on how well they performed in the experiment
To collect participant credit card numbers for billing

questions.explanation: Debriefing dehoaxes participants, explains the rationale for deception, answers questions, and mitigates any distress.

questions.question: In research involving minors (under 18), what is the ethical requirement regarding consent?

options.text: Minors can sign legal consent forms without parental notification
Parents or legal guardians provide formal consent, and the child provides affirmative assent
No consent is required as long as the school principal agrees
Only children who can pass an adult reading test are allowed in studies

questions.explanation: For minors, guardians provide legally binding informed consent, while the child provides assent (developmentally appropriate agreement).

questions.question: What is the key distinction between anonymity and confidentiality in data collection?

options.text: They are exact synonyms with no practical difference
Anonymity means no identifying information is ever collected; confidentiality means identifiers are collected but protected from disclosure
Confidentiality means data is deleted immediately after collection
Anonymity applies only to animal research

questions.explanation: Under anonymity, even the researcher cannot link responses to identities; under confidentiality, the researcher possesses identifying keys but keeps them secure.

questions.question: Which of the following constitutes scientific fabrication?

options.text: Forgetting to cite a reference in a bibliography
Inventing fictional data points and publishing them as genuine empirical results
Using a two-tailed t-test instead of a one-tailed t-test
Using an outdated computer operating system in the laboratory

questions.explanation: Fabrication is the outright invention of fake data or observations.

questions.question: Manipulating research materials or omitting select data without scientific justification so the study conforms to a preferred hypothesis is known as:

options.text: Falsification
Fabrication
Triangulation
Deduction

questions.explanation: Selectively altering, manipulating, or omitting data to distort results constitutes falsification.

questions.question: What committee oversees and approves research protocols involving non-human animals in academic institutions?

options.text: IRB
IACUC (Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee)
FDA
APA Ethics Division exclusively

questions.explanation: The IACUC (Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee) is responsible for overseeing animal research ethics and welfare.

questions.question: In the 3Rs framework of animal research, what does 'Reduction' signify?

options.text: Decreasing the size of animal cages
Using experimental designs and statistics that minimize the number of animals required to obtain valid data
Reducing the salaries of laboratory veterinarians
Cutting the length of journal articles

questions.explanation: Reduction focuses on using optimized statistical strategies and study designs to use as few animals as scientifically necessary.

questions.question: In the 3Rs framework, replacing living animal models with tissue cultures, computer algorithms, or human neuroimaging is an example of:

options.text: Replacement
Refinement
Reduction
Replication

questions.explanation: Replacement refers to adopting non-animal methods (e.g., in vitro, computational simulations) in place of live animals.

questions.question: What critical oversight breakdown occurred during Philip Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment?

options.text: Participants were given counterfeit currency
The lead investigator served as Prison Superintendent, compromising objective ethical oversight
The study was published without statistical graphs
The participants were all under age 10

questions.explanation: Zimbardo's dual role as lead researcher and prison superintendent compromised his objectivity, causing him to ignore escalating emotional abuse until an outside observer intervened.

questions.question: Why is offering an excessively large cash reward (e.g., $10,000 for a 1-hour study) considered ethically problematic?

options.text: Because psychology departments never have that much funding
It exerts 'undue influence' that may cause economically desperate people to ignore severe risks
Because the IRS taxes all research compensation above $50
It causes all participants to answer questions in reverse order

questions.explanation: Disproportionate financial incentives constitute undue influence, blinding vulnerable participants to real experimental hazards.

questions.question: What is the primary ethical purpose of a 'Certificate of Confidentiality' issued by federal agencies like the NIH?

options.text: To allow researchers to conceal fraudulent financial statements
To protect researchers from being forced by courts or subpoenas to disclose sensitive participant data (e.g., illegal drug use)
To prevent other scientists from replicating the research
To eliminate the need for informed consent documents

questions.explanation: Certificates of Confidentiality protect participants by legally shielding identifiable sensitive research records from court subpoenas.

questions.question: If a participant signs an informed consent document but begins to feel overwhelmed and states they want to leave during minute 10, what must the researcher do?

options.text: Insist they finish because they signed a binding contract
Immediately stop the procedure and allow the participant to withdraw without penalty
Charge the participant for the cost of laboratory materials
Lock the laboratory door until the final questionnaire is answered

questions.explanation: Participants retain the absolute, unconditional right to withdraw from a study at any time without penalty or forfeit of compensation.
